passages.title: On Letters
passages.text: It is tempting to see the decline of handwritten letters as a simple loss. Yet letters were never merely vessels of affection; they were also instruments of control, used to issue orders, settle debts and, occasionally, to deceive. What we mourn, perhaps, is not the letter itself but the slowness it imposed — a slowness that forced writers to weigh their words. Digital messages need not be careless, but their speed makes carelessness easy.

passages.title: The Cartographer's Dilemma
passages.text: When the Royal Society commissioned a new map of the kingdom, it expected precision. What it received was something more troubling. The cartographer, a meticulous woman named Orla Venn, had walked every road herself and discovered that several villages shown on the old maps no longer existed, while others had grown into towns that appeared nowhere. Worse, three 'rivers' turned out to be dry ditches, drawn decades earlier to strengthen land claims. Venn's map was accurate, but it was also politically explosive: it undermined the boundaries on which several noble estates depended. The Society shelved it for a generation. Her story is a reminder that maps are never merely descriptive; they are arguments about who owns the world.

passages.title: In Praise of Boredom
passages.text: We have engineered boredom out of our lives. Every queue, commute and pause is now filled by a glowing screen. Yet psychologists increasingly argue that boredom is not a malfunction but a signal: a prompt to seek something more meaningful. In one study, participants who had first completed a dull task, copying numbers from a phone directory, went on to generate more creative uses for a plastic cup than those who had not. The researchers do not claim that tedium is pleasant, only that it may be productive. The difficulty is that the payoff comes later, while the discomfort is immediate, and a phone offers instant relief.

passages.title: The Octopus Who Escaped
passages.text: Inky, a common New Zealand octopus, had lived contentedly at the National Aquarium for two years when, one night, he staged what staff later called 'the great escape'. Having squeezed through a small gap left at the top of his tank, he slid across the floor and slipped down a fifty-metre drainpipe that led straight to the sea. Keepers were not entirely surprised: octopuses are notorious escape artists, capable of unscrewing jar lids and, in some aquariums, of switching off lights they find irritating by squirting water at them. Rather than replacing Inky, the aquarium decided to celebrate him, and visitor numbers rose sharply in the months that followed.

passages.title: In Praise of Boredom
passages.text: We tend to treat boredom as a problem to be solved, usually by reaching for a screen. Yet a growing body of research suggests that boredom may be quietly useful. In one well-known study, participants who first spent fifteen minutes copying numbers from a phone book came up with markedly more creative uses for a pair of plastic cups than those who went straight to the task. Psychologists believe that when the mind has nothing to engage it, it begins to wander, making unexpected connections. This is not to say that endless boredom is healthy; rather, the occasional empty afternoon may be worth protecting.

passages.title: The Girl Who Taught a Village to Code
passages.text: When the only computer at her school in rural Kenya broke down, twelve-year-old Wanjiru refused to let the coding club die. Instead, she taught her classmates programming logic using cardboard 'robots', pebbles and chalk grids drawn in the playground. Her unplugged lessons proved so popular that younger children began turning up after school, and eventually parents asked to join too. When a charity later donated ten laptops, the teachers found that Wanjiru's students picked up real programming languages far faster than expected. 'They already understood how to think like a computer,' one teacher remarked. 'All they lacked was the machine.'

passages.title: Ask the Editor: Are Book Reviews by Kids Worth Reading?
passages.text: Dear Editor, my class has started writing book reviews for our school website, but my older brother says nobody cares what an eleven-year-old thinks. Is he right? — Leo | Dear Leo, your brother couldn't be more mistaken. Publishers increasingly seek out young reviewers precisely because adults are notoriously poor at predicting what children will love. A good review, whatever the writer's age, does three things: it explains what the book is about without spoiling the ending, it gives honest reasons for the reviewer's opinion, and it helps readers decide whether the book is for them. Keep writing, and you might be surprised who's reading.

passages.title: The Mystery of the Singing Sands
passages.text: In a handful of deserts around the world, sand dunes produce a deep humming sound, sometimes loud enough to be heard ten kilometres away. Marco Polo described the noise in the thirteenth century, attributing it to desert spirits. Scientists have long argued over the real cause. The current consensus is that the sound occurs when dry grains of a particular size avalanche down a slope in unison, their collisions synchronising like the members of a choir. Curiously, the note each dune 'sings' depends not on the dune's size but on the size of its grains, which is why sand from the same dune hums the same note even in a laboratory.

passages.text: Dear parents, I am delighted to report that our robot, Sparky, finished third out of forty teams at the regional championships. This is all the more remarkable given that, two days before the event, a software update wiped most of the team's code. Rather than panicking, the students divided the work, rewrote the essential functions overnight and stripped out every feature that wasn't strictly necessary. Ironically, the judges praised Sparky's 'elegant simplicity'. We now qualify for the national finals in March, for which we will need help with transport and, as ever, snacks.

passages.title: The Art of Getting Lost
passages.text: In an age of satellite navigation, getting genuinely lost has become something of a rarity, and some psychologists think we are poorer for it. Studies of London taxi drivers, who must memorise thousands of streets, found that the part of the brain associated with spatial memory grew measurably larger over the course of their training. Habitual satnav users, by contrast, show far less activity in that region while travelling. None of this means we should abandon technology; but switching off the app occasionally, and trusting our own sense of direction, may keep our mental maps in better shape.

passages.title: Notes from the School Beekeeping Club
passages.text: When Ms Adeyemi first proposed keeping bees on the school roof, the reaction from parents was, to put it diplomatically, mixed. Three years on, the club has thirty members, two thriving hives and a waiting list. Members wear full protective suits and are never allowed near the hives unsupervised. Contrary to popular belief, honeybees are rarely aggressive unless their hive is threatened; in three years, there has been only one sting, and that was Ms Adeyemi herself, who had forgotten her gloves. Last year's honey sold out at the summer fair within an hour, raising enough to buy a third hive.

notes.they only sting teachers: The teacher's sting is a joke, not a rule.

questions.q: What was the honey money used for?
questions.explain: 'Raising enough to buy a third hive.'

notes.more gloves: Gloves are a joke about the sting.

passages.title: The Museum of Broken Friendships
passages.text: In a small gallery in Zagreb, visitors wander past exhibits that have nothing in common except that each represents the end of a relationship: a teddy bear, a toaster, a single roller skate. Each object is donated anonymously, along with a short story explaining its significance. What began as an art project between two friends has since toured more than fifty countries. Curators say the appeal lies in the paradox at the museum's heart: though every story is about loss, visitors frequently leave feeling comforted, reassured that heartache is universal.

questions.q: What links the exhibits?
options: each marks the end of a relationship
questions.explain: 'Each represents the end of a relationship.'

questions.q: What comes with each object?
questions.explain: 'Along with a short story explaining its significance.'

questions.q: How did the museum start?
questions.explain: 'What began as an art project between two friends.'

questions.q: What is the 'paradox' the curators mention?
options: the museum is small but famous
the objects are cheap but valued
questions.explain: 'Though every story is about loss, visitors frequently leave feeling comforted.'

questions.q: Why do visitors feel reassured?
questions.explain: 'Reassured that heartache is universal.'

passages.title: Should Homework Be Banned?
passages.text: Every few years, a headline announces that some school has abolished homework, and the debate reignites. Research offers less clarity than either side would like. For primary-age children, studies find little link between homework and achievement; for older students, a moderate amount, roughly one to two hours a night, appears beneficial, but returns diminish sharply beyond that. Much depends on the type of task: practising a skill already taught seems more useful than tackling new material alone. Perhaps the question, then, is not whether homework should exist, but what it should be for.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the research?
options: it isn't as clear as people want
there is no research at all
questions.explain: 'Research offers less clarity than either side would like.'

questions.q: What do studies find for young children?
options: they need two hours a night
questions.explain: 'Little link between homework and achievement.'

notes.homework greatly improves results: Little link, not a big improvement.
notes.they need two hours a night: Two hours is for older students.

questions.q: What does 'returns diminish sharply' mean?
questions.explain: Beyond two hours, each extra hour brings much less benefit.

notes.students hand in less work: It's about benefit, not handing in.

questions.q: Which homework seems most useful?
questions.explain: 'Practising a skill already taught seems more useful.'

questions.q: How does the writer reframe the debate?
questions.explain: 'Not whether homework should exist, but what it should be for.'

passages.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
passages.text: When a storm knocked out power across the island for three days, my family discovered that we had no idea how to entertain ourselves without electricity. The first evening was a disaster of sulking and dead phones. By the second, however, my dad had dug out a battered board game, my sister was reading by candlelight, and I'd started writing a story in a notebook I'd forgotten I owned. When the lights flickered back on, there was a moment of genuine disappointment. We now hold a 'blackout night' once a month, though I suspect my sister cheats by charging her phone in secret.

questions.q: How long did the power cut last?
questions.explain: 'For three days.'

notes.one evening: The first evening was just the start.

questions.q: How did the first evening go?
questions.explain: 'A disaster of sulking and dead phones.'

questions.q: What did the writer start doing?
questions.explain: 'I'd started writing a story in a notebook.'

notes.playing a board game alone: Dad got the board game out.

questions.q: How did the family feel when power returned?
questions.explain: 'A moment of genuine disappointment.'

questions.q: What does the writer suspect?
options: the sister secretly uses her phone
the power will go off again
questions.explain: 'My sister cheats by charging her phone in secret.'

notes.nobody enjoys blackout night: They hold it monthly by choice.

passages.title: Why We Remember Embarrassing Moments
passages.text: Most of us can recall, in excruciating detail, a moment of embarrassment from years ago, while countless pleasant afternoons have vanished without trace. Psychologists attribute this to the brain's threat-detection system: emotionally charged events, particularly social blunders, are tagged as important and stored more vividly, presumably because, for our ancestors, being rejected by the group could be genuinely dangerous. The good news is that other people remember our embarrassing moments far less clearly than we do; most, in fact, were too preoccupied with their own to notice.

questions.q: What contrast is drawn in the first sentence?
options: we keep the bad, lose the good
we forget everything after a year
questions.explain: Embarrassment recalled 'in excruciating detail'; pleasant afternoons 'vanished'.

questions.q: Why does the brain store these moments vividly?
options: it treats them as possible threats
we talk about them a lot
questions.explain: 'The brain's threat-detection system… tagged as important.'

questions.q: Why might this have mattered for our ancestors?
options: rejection by the group was dangerous
they had no way to write things down
questions.explain: 'Being rejected by the group could be genuinely dangerous.'

questions.q: What does 'presumably' show about the explanation?
questions.explain: 'Presumably' = probably, a reasonable assumption.

questions.q: What is the 'good news'?
questions.explain: 'Other people remember our embarrassing moments far less clearly.'

passages.title: The Robot That Learned to Fail
passages.text: When the Greenfield Robotics Club built their first maze-solving robot, it crashed into the very first wall and spun helplessly in circles. Most teams would have rewritten the program from scratch. Instead, their mentor, a retired engineer called Mr Basu, insisted they keep a 'failure diary', recording every crash and what they thought had caused it. The diary grew to forty pages. Gradually, a pattern emerged: almost every crash happened when the robot turned left, which led them to a faulty sensor rather than a flaw in their code. By the regional final, the robot completed the maze in under a minute. Asked about their success, the team captain was quick to credit the diary rather than the robot.

questions.q: What would most teams have done, according to the writer?
questions.explain: 'Most teams would have rewritten the program from scratch.'

notes.kept a failure diary: That's what this team did instead.
notes.replaced the robot's sensors: That happened only after the pattern emerged.

questions.q: Why did Mr Basu want a diary?
options: to spot the causes of mistakes
to punish members who made careless mistakes
questions.explain: 'Recording every crash and what they thought had caused it.'

questions.q: What did the diary eventually reveal?
questions.explain: 'Led them to a faulty sensor rather than a flaw in their code.'

notes.a mistake in the code: 'Rather than a flaw in their code.'
notes.that left turns are impossible: Left turns just exposed the sensor.

questions.q: What does the captain's answer suggest?
options: the method mattered more than the machine
the robot itself deserved all the credit for winning
the diary was a waste of time
Mr Basu should get the prize
questions.explain: 'Quick to credit the diary rather than the robot.'

notes.the robot itself deserved all the credit: The diary gets the credit, not the robot.

passages.title: Tardigrades: The Toughest Animals on Earth
passages.text: At barely half a millimetre long, tardigrades – affectionately nicknamed 'water bears' – hardly look like champions. Yet these eight-legged creatures can survive conditions that would kill virtually anything else. When their surroundings dry out, they curl into a ball, lose almost all the water in their bodies and effectively switch themselves off, sometimes for decades. In this state, they have withstood temperatures close to absolute zero, crushing pressures and even a trip into open space aboard a satellite. Remarkably, when rehydrated, many simply carry on as if nothing had happened. Scientists hope that understanding how they protect their cells could, one day, help keep vaccines safe without refrigeration.

questions.q: What does the first sentence imply?
options: they are very easy to see without a microscope
questions.explain: 'Hardly look like champions. Yet…' — they are far tougher than they appear.

questions.q: What do tardigrades do when things dry out?
options: drink as much as they can
questions.explain: 'Lose almost all the water in their bodies and effectively switch themselves off.'

notes.drink as much as they can: They lose water, not drink it.

questions.q: Which has a tardigrade NOT survived, according to the text?
questions.explain: Lava isn't mentioned; the others are all listed.

notes.extreme cold: 'Temperatures close to absolute zero' are listed.
notes.a journey into space: 'A trip into open space' is listed.

questions.q: What does 'as if nothing had happened' suggest?
questions.explain: 'Many simply carry on' = they return to normal.

notes.they need weeks to wake: 'Simply carry on' suggests no long delay.

questions.q: How might tardigrades help people?
options: by keeping medicines usable without fridges
by cleaning dirty water in rivers and lakes
questions.explain: 'Help keep vaccines safe without refrigeration.'

notes.by travelling to other planets: Their space trip was an experiment.
notes.by curing all diseases: Only vaccines are mentioned, and only 'one day'.

passages.title: Confessions of a Reluctant Goalkeeper
passages.text: Nobody chooses to be a goalkeeper at the age of ten; you are chosen, usually because you were the last to arrive at practice. That, at least, is how it happened to me. For the first season, I regarded the goal as a kind of punishment, a place where I could only be blamed and never praised. It was a single match that changed my mind. We were losing two–nil when I saved a penalty, and the whole team came sprinting back to hug me. I realised then that a goalkeeper doesn't just stop goals; they can change the mood of an entire side. I've been in goal ever since, and I wouldn't swap it for anything – not even for the chance to score.

questions.q: According to the writer, how do children become goalkeepers?
options: by bad luck rather than choice
by being the most talented player in the squad
questions.explain: 'You are chosen, usually because you were the last to arrive.'

questions.q: How did the writer see the role at first?
questions.explain: 'A place where I could only be blamed and never praised.'

notes.as an honour: They saw it as 'a kind of punishment'.
notes.as a chance to score: Goalkeepers rarely score; they say so.

questions.q: What was the score when the penalty was saved?
options: the team was two goals down
questions.explain: 'We were losing two–nil.'

questions.q: What did the writer learn from that match?
questions.explain: 'They can change the mood of an entire side.'

notes.attackers deserve more praise: The point is the keeper's importance.
notes.it's better to arrive early: That's a joke from the start, not the lesson.

questions.q: What does the final sentence emphasise?
options: the writer's secret wish to score goals one day
questions.explain: 'I wouldn't swap it for anything – not even for the chance to score.'

notes.the writer's secret wish to score goals: They'd give up scoring to stay in goal.

passages.title: Speedrunning: Racing Through Games
passages.text: To most players, finishing a video game is the goal. To speedrunners, it is merely the starting point. These dedicated gamers compete to complete games as fast as humanly possible, often spending thousands of hours shaving fractions of a second off their times. Some exploit glitches – mistakes in the game's code – to pass through walls or skip whole levels, which purists consider cheating and others regard as a legitimate skill. What surprises many outsiders is how cooperative the community is: rivals routinely share newly discovered tricks, knowing full well this may cost them their own records. Every year, charity marathons of speedrunning raise millions, proving that watching someone else play can be strangely gripping.

questions.q: How do speedrunners view finishing a game?
options: as too easy to bother with
questions.explain: 'To speedrunners, it is merely the starting point.'

notes.as the final aim: That's how most players see it.
notes.as too easy to bother with: They spend thousands of hours on it.

questions.q: What does the text say about using glitches?
questions.explain: 'Which purists consider cheating and others regard as a legitimate skill.'

questions.q: What surprises outsiders?
options: players keep their newest tricks to themselves
questions.explain: 'Rivals routinely share newly discovered tricks.'

notes.records are rarely broken: Shaving seconds means records do fall.

questions.q: What does 'knowing full well' suggest about the sharing?
options: it's a way of showing off
questions.explain: They share although they know they may lose their records.

notes.it's accidental: They know the risk, so it's deliberate.
notes.it's a way of showing off: The point is generosity, not boasting.

questions.q: What do charity marathons show, according to the writer?
questions.explain: 'Watching someone else play can be strangely gripping.'

passages.title: The Lost Property Office of the Starlight Library
passages.text: Every library has a lost property box, but the Starlight Library's is a whole office, staffed by a tortoise named Hollis who has worked there for three hundred years. The things left behind are rarely umbrellas. Readers have abandoned half-finished wishes, forgotten nicknames and, on one memorable occasion, an entire thunderstorm, which Hollis kept in a jam jar until its owner returned. Apprentices are warned never to open the cabinet marked 'Lost Tempers', a lesson the current apprentice, Tamsin, learned the hard way. Yet Hollis insists that the saddest objects are not the strangest ones but the ordinary bookmarks, each marking a story that somebody never came back to finish.

questions.q: What is unusual about the lost property, compared with a normal library?
questions.explain: 'The things left behind are rarely umbrellas… half-finished wishes… an entire thunderstorm.'

notes.the box is very small: It's a whole office, not a box.

questions.q: What happened to the thunderstorm?
options: it was stored until someone claimed it
Hollis threw it out of the window into the sky
questions.explain: 'Kept in a jam jar until its owner returned.'

notes.it escaped into the library: It was kept safe in a jar.
notes.Tamsin let it out: Tamsin's mistake was a different cabinet.

questions.q: What can we infer about Tamsin?
options: she has worked there for centuries
she lost her temper with Hollis
questions.explain: 'A lesson the current apprentice, Tamsin, learned the hard way.'

notes.she lost her temper with Hollis: She opened the cabinet; we aren't told she lost her own temper.

questions.q: Why does Hollis find bookmarks the saddest objects?
questions.explain: 'Each marking a story that somebody never came back to finish.'

notes.they are the strangest things: 'Not the strangest ones but the ordinary bookmarks.'

passages.title: Should Every School Teach Chess?
passages.text: Chess enthusiasts have long claimed that the game makes children cleverer, and several countries now include it in their primary school timetable. The evidence, however, is more mixed than its champions admit. Some studies have found that pupils who play chess improve in maths, but others suggest that these gains fade within a year or so, or that they appear only among children who already enjoyed the game. What seems clearer is that chess teaches patience and the ability to lose gracefully. Perhaps, then, the strongest case for chess in schools is not that it turns pupils into geniuses, but that it gives them a calm, shared challenge in an increasingly hurried world.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about chess enthusiasts?
options: most of them are scientists who study children
questions.explain: 'The evidence… is more mixed than its champions admit.'

notes.they are always right: The evidence doesn't fully support them.

questions.q: What do some studies suggest about maths gains?
options: they appear immediately in all pupils
questions.explain: 'These gains fade within a year or so.'

questions.q: According to the writer, what is more certain?
options: chess is faster than other games
questions.explain: 'What seems clearer is that chess teaches patience and the ability to lose gracefully.'

questions.q: What is the writer's overall position?
options: neutral, because the evidence is too mixed to decide
questions.explain: 'The strongest case… is not that it turns pupils into geniuses, but that it gives them a calm, shared challenge.'

notes.strongly against chess: They suggest a 'strongest case' for it.
notes.neutral, because the evidence is too mix: They reach a view at the end.

passages.title: A Diary from the Space Station
passages.text: Day 12. I still haven't got used to sleeping upright in a sleeping bag strapped to the wall, though the crew assure me that by the end of the month I won't be able to sleep any other way. Eating is a performance in itself: crumbs are banned, because they drift into equipment, so bread has been replaced by tortillas. This morning we watched sixteen sunrises in a single day – it never stops being astonishing. If I'm honest, though, what I miss most isn't anything grand. It's rain. I would happily trade one of those sunrises for ten minutes standing in a proper downpour back home.

questions.q: What do the crew predict about sleeping?
options: the writer will get used to it
the writer will never adapt to sleeping on the wall
questions.explain: 'By the end of the month I won't be able to sleep any other way.'

notes.sleeping will get harder: They think it will become natural.

questions.q: Why are tortillas eaten instead of bread?
options: they don't leave bits floating around
the crew dislike the taste of bread in space
questions.explain: 'Crumbs are banned, because they drift into equipment.'

questions.q: How does the writer feel about the sunrises?
questions.explain: 'It never stops being astonishing.'

notes.they happen too rarely: Sixteen a day is very often.

questions.q: What does the ending reveal?
options: it often rains inside the space station
the writer wants to go home now
questions.explain: 'What I miss most isn't anything grand. It's rain.'

notes.it often rains inside the space station: Rain is what they miss, so it doesn't rain there.

passages.title: Hedgehog Highways
passages.text: Hedgehogs may travel up to two kilometres a night in search of food and mates, but in modern towns their journeys are increasingly blocked by solid fences and walls. Numbers in some countries have fallen dramatically, and while there are several causes, wildlife charities believe that lost routes are a major one. Their solution is refreshingly simple: cut a hole about the size of a CD in the bottom of your garden fence. Linked together, these gaps form so-called 'hedgehog highways'. One school in Bristol persuaded every house on its street to take part, and within a year night-time cameras had recorded hedgehogs in gardens where none had been seen for a decade.

questions.q: What is a major problem for hedgehogs, according to charities?
options: a lack of food in towns
questions.explain: 'Their journeys are increasingly blocked by solid fences and walls.'

notes.a lack of food in towns: They search for food, but the problem is access.

questions.q: What does 'refreshingly simple' suggest about the solution?
questions.explain: A hole the size of a CD is quick and easy, and the writer welcomes this.

notes.it's expensive: Cost isn't mentioned, and it's just a hole.

questions.q: How big should the hole be?
options: roughly as wide as a CD
the size of a hedgehog's nose
questions.explain: 'A hole about the size of a CD.'

notes.two kilometres wide: Two kilometres is their nightly distance.

questions.q: What did the Bristol cameras show?
questions.explain: 'Recorded hedgehogs in gardens where none had been seen for a decade.'

passages.title: The Science Fair Judge
passages.text: I had always assumed that judging a science fair would be easy – you simply pick the project with the most impressive results. My first year as a student judge cured me of that idea. The project that lingered in my mind wasn't the glossy one about rocket fuel, whose author couldn't explain half of what was on his poster. It was a modest experiment on whether snails prefer cucumber or lettuce. The girl behind it had tested her hypothesis three times, admitted that one result contradicted the others and suggested why. Her conclusion was hardly earth-shattering, but her honesty about the messy bits was exactly what science is meant to be.

questions.q: What did the writer believe before judging?
questions.explain: 'You simply pick the project with the most impressive results.'

notes.judging would be very hard: They assumed it would be easy.

questions.q: What was wrong with the rocket fuel project?
options: its creator didn't understand it fully
its poster was dull and badly organised
questions.explain: 'Whose author couldn't explain half of what was on his poster.'

questions.q: How did the girl deal with the result that didn't fit?
options: she repeated the test until it fitted
questions.explain: 'Admitted that one result contradicted the others and suggested why.'

notes.she repeated the test until it fitted: She tested three times, then reported honestly.

questions.q: What is the writer's attitude to the snail project?
options: it was too simple to count
it should have been about rockets
questions.explain: 'Hardly earth-shattering, but her honesty… was exactly what science is meant to be.'

notes.it should have been about rockets: The rocket project was the weaker one.

questions.q: What does 'cured me of that idea' mean?
questions.explain: Being cured of an idea = no longer believing it.
